result.summary: Agamemnon, unable to sleep, rouses Nestor and the chiefs, who hold a council beyond the trench. Diomed and Ulysses volunteer to spy, capture and kill the Trojan scout Dolon, then slaughter the sleeping Thracians, kill Rhesus and bring back his horses.

scenes.title: Sleepless Agamemnon rouses the chiefs
scenes.summary: Agamemnon and Menelaus rise in anxiety. Agamemnon consults Nestor, and they begin waking the leaders.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans face destruction by Hector and Jove's favour to the Trojans.

scenes.title: Waking Ulysses and Diomed
scenes.summary: Nestor wakes Ulysses and Diomed, and the chiefs inspect the guards and gather beyond the trench.
scenes.stakes: Life and death are balanced for the Achaeans.

scenes.title: Council and choice of spies
scenes.summary: Nestor asks for a volunteer scout. Diomed chooses Ulysses, they are armed and pray to Minerva.
scenes.stakes: The two spies risk death in the enemy camp at night.

scenes.title: Hector and Dolon's bargain
scenes.summary: Hector seeks a spy, and Dolon volunteers in return for Achilles' horses.
scenes.stakes: Dolon risks his life for a reward he will never receive.

scenes.title: Capture and death of Dolon
scenes.summary: Ulysses and Diomed catch Dolon, learn the camp's layout and about Rhesus, then Diomed kills him.
scenes.stakes: Dolon's life; for the Greeks, the secrecy of their raid.

scenes.title: Slaughter of the Thracians
scenes.summary: Diomed kills Rhesus and twelve men while Ulysses takes the horses. Minerva warns them, and Apollo rouses Hippocoon.
scenes.stakes: Discovery and pursuit by roused Trojans.

scenes.title: Return and offering to Minerva
scenes.summary: The heroes return with the horses, are praised by Nestor, bathe and pour wine to Minerva.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of the goddess Minerva (Greek Athena).

notable_quotes.reason: Nestor's vivid image of the Achaeans' peril, balanced on a razor's edge.
Diomed's reasoning for why two men are better than one.

analysis.text: The night expedition contrasts anxious leadership with cunning and daring, and shows Minerva's favour for Ulysses and Diomed.
Book 10, the Doloneia, has long been suspected by scholars of being a later addition to the Iliad.

legacy.text: Euripides' play Rhesus retells the night raid on the Thracian king.

fun_facts.text: The boar's-tusk helmet in this book matches Mycenaean helmets found by archaeologists.

language_notes.text: "Juno's lord" is Jove (the Greek Zeus), husband of Juno (Hera); his lightning was read as an omen of storm or war.
"Any way of the Achaeans from destruction" is elliptical: any way to save the Achaeans from destruction.
"Casque" is an archaic word for a helmet.
"Exploit" here means to scout or spy out; it is not used in the modern sense of taking advantage.
"Give each all titular observance" means address each man with his full titles and due respect, setting aside rank and pride.
"For his age stayed him not" means old age did not keep Nestor from going to battle.
"I am at sea" is figurative: Agamemnon is adrift and uncertain, lacking a plan.
"Peer of gods in counsel" is a fixed epithet meaning equal to the gods in wisdom and advice.
"Take it not amiss" means do not be offended or take it badly.
Spears stand upright on their "butts": the spike at the shaft's lower end was driven into the ground to hold the spear upright.
"Upbraiding" means scolding or reproaching.
"Edge of a razor" is a proverbial image for a situation that could tip either way.
Refers to the previous day's fighting, when Hector drove the Achaeans back to their ships and night ended the battle.
"Worsted" means defeated or got the better of. "Achaeans" is a general name for the Greeks, as is "Argives".
"Clan-gatherings" are communal feasts of the leading men; being invited as guest to them was a mark of honour.
"Held their peace" means they stayed silent, since nobody wanted to speak first about so dangerous a task.
Agamemnon warns Diomed not to choose a lesser man out of "delicacy" (reluctance to offend) merely because a better man has higher rank.
"The stars have gone forward" means the constellations have moved across the sky, showing most of the night has passed.
A "skull-cap" here is a plain helmet of bull's hide, with no peak (visor) and no crest (plume).
Autolycus was a famous thief, said to be grandfather of Ulysses on his mother's side. The helmet's history is told as a chain of owners.
A heron on the right was a lucky omen. The heron was a bird sacred to Minerva, so its cry signals her favour.
Tydeus went to Thebes as envoy before the war of the Seven against Thebes; Diomed recalls this earlier feat and Minerva's help.
"Cadmeians" are the people of Thebes, named after its founder Cadmus.
"As heretofore" means as they have been up to now; "to boot" means in addition.
"Exploit" here means to explore or spy out the ships, not to take advantage of them.
"Bedight" is archaic for adorned or decked out.
Holding up the sceptre while swearing made the oath formal; Hector invokes Jove, guardian of oaths. The horses are Achilles', who is still alive, so the promise is rash.
"Bootless" means useless or without effect; the oath could never be fulfilled.
An "overall" is an outer covering; Dolon wears a wolfskin as a disguise for night scouting.
The furrow comparison gives a rough distance: the gap Dolon had gained, like the extra length a mule can plow over oxen in the same time.
"Bronze-bedizened" means gaudily decked out with bronze; "heretofore" means until now.
"Descendant of Aeacus" means Achilles, whose father Peleus was Aeacus's son. His immortal horses were a gift from the gods and could be handled only by him.
This list names Trojan allies from Asia Minor and Thrace; the catalogue shows the camp is divided by tribe and that the allies are not closely guarded.
"Bedight" is archaic for adorned; "meet" means fitting.
Touching the beard was a gesture of supplication, a plea for mercy. Dolon's head speaks on after death in the sense that it falls mid-sentence.
Hanging spoils on a tree as an offering to a god of war was a customary thanks; Minerva (the Greek Athene) has helped them.
"Yoke of horses" means a pair of horses harnessed together to pull a chariot.
"Dally" means to waste time; Ulysses urges Diomed not to linger over the armour.
"Son of Tydeus" is a patronymic: it names Diomed by his father.
"The seed of Oeneus" refers to Diomed, whose father Tydeus was Oeneus's son. The dream is Diomed himself, appearing as an omen of death.
"Kept no blind look-out" is an understatement meaning Apollo watched closely and noticed at once.
"Nothing loth" means not unwilling; the horses ran eagerly.
"Shall I guess right or wrong?" is a modest hedge: Nestor offers his hunch while admitting he may be mistaken.
Gerene is a place associated with Nestor; "knight" here means a horseman or charioteer, not a medieval knight.
"Conversant with" means well acquainted with; Nestor says he knows the Trojans from frequent fighting at the front.
"Achaean" is another name for the Greeks, used interchangeably with Argives.
"Spoils of Dolon" are the armour stripped from the Trojan spy Dolon, whom Diomed and Ulysses captured and killed earlier in this book.
A "drink-offering" is a libation: wine poured out as a religious gift to a god.

context_notes.text: Ilius is Ilium, another name for Troy. The Trojan watchfires show the enemy camped on the plain, close to the Achaean ships.
Menelaus is Agamemnon's brother. The war was fought to recover his wife Helen, so the Argives sailed on his account.
Hector, the Trojan champion, has driven the Achaeans back to their ships. Agamemnon notes he is mortal, with no god for a parent.
Nestor is the oldest Achaean leader, respected for his wisdom and counsel.
Achilles has withdrawn from the fighting over his quarrel with Agamemnon. Nestor hints that his return would turn the war.
Nestor is the oldest Achaean leader, king of Pylos, famed for his counsel. Gerene is an epithet-place linked to him.
Diomed, son of Tydeus, is one of the Achaeans' strongest warriors and sleeps armed and ready among his men.
Ajax is the great Achaean warrior; the son of Phyleus is Meges, leader of the men from Dulichium.
A lion skin is a warrior's cloak, signaling strength and ferocity.
Pallas Minerva (the Greek Athene) is goddess of wisdom and war, and Ulysses' special protector throughout the poem.
The aegis was Jove's (Zeus's) shield or goatskin cape, which Minerva also carries; "aegis-bearing" is a regular title for him.
An unbroken heifer, never yoked, was considered a pure and especially fitting sacrifice, and gilded horns made it more costly.
Heralds were respected officials who carried messages and presided over assemblies; Dolon's father Eumedes was a famous one.
Achilles, son of Peleus, is sitting out the war in anger at Agamemnon. His divine horses are an extraordinary prize.
Minerva favours Diomed and Ulysses throughout this night raid, and here she makes sure Diomed wins the glory of the first strike.
The tomb of Ilus, an ancestor of the Trojan kings, stood on the plain and served as a landmark and meeting place.
Dolon had disguised himself in animal skins for his night spying, so these are his gear and the spoils taken from him.
Dolon was a Trojan spy captured earlier in the night. He revealed where Rhesus and his famous horses were camped before being killed.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) favours Diomed and Ulysses throughout this night raid.
Apollo (the Greek god) supported the Trojans and opposed Minerva's help to the Greeks.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is Jove's daughter and goddess of wisdom and war; she often favours Ulysses and Diomed.
Thrace lay north of Troy. Its king Rhesus had come as a Trojan ally, and his famous horses were taken.
Washing in the sea and then in baths was a normal way to clean up after exertion before eating.

literary_notes.text: Agamemnon's sighs are compared to Jove's lightning, which warns of storm or war, so his distress reads as an omen.
The Trojan fires, pipes and humming voices contrast with the silent Achaean camp, intensifying Agamemnon's dread.
The lion skin that reaches his feet shows Agamemnon's royal bearing and the size of his presence.
Menelaus' dressing in a panther skin, helmet and spear echoes his brother's, linking the two men's shared anxiety.
Agamemnon defends his brother kindly, showing loyalty and a more humane side.
The flashing bronze spears are compared to Jove's lightning, lending the sleeping camp a sense of divine power.
Calling Nestor's heart "of iron" conveys his tireless endurance despite his age.
The wakeful Achaeans are likened to sheepdogs alerted by a wild beast, conveying their tense vigilance against the Trojans.
"Diomed of the loud war-cry" is a fixed Homeric epithet, stressing his role as a battle leader.
Diomed's practical remark shows him as bold yet sensible, aware that teamwork improves judgment.
Passing safely "through fire itself" exaggerates to express Diomed's trust in Ulysses' cleverness.
The long history of the helmet pauses the action and gives the object weight, linking Ulysses to the cunning thief Autolycus.
Comparing the pair to prowling lions conveys their stealth and ferocity as they enter a field of corpses.
Dolon's ugliness, speed and wealth, as an only son among sisters, sketch a man who is spoiled and eager to prove himself.
The narrator tells us the oath is worthless, so Dolon's eagerness rests on a promise that cannot be kept.
The narrator announces Dolon's failure in advance, replacing suspense with dread about how he will fall.
The two pursuers are compared to hounds chasing a doe or hare, making Dolon the helpless prey.
Diomed's deliberately missed throw is a threat, not an attack; it frightens Dolon into stopping while keeping him alive for questioning.
Dolon blames Hector's flattery, showing him as greedy, weak and quick to betray his own side.
Dolon hopes his information will buy his life, but Diomed argues that it only shows him to be a dangerous enemy who must die.
Diomed is compared to a lion among unguarded flocks, stressing his ferocity and the helplessness of the sleeping Thracians.
Ulysses forgetting the whip and using his bow shows him improvising calmly, a resourceful man more than a frenzied killer.
The horses fly onward "as though of their own free will," giving them eagerness and a will of their own.
Nestor's hope and fear about Diomed and Ulysses build brief suspense before their safe return is revealed.
Comparing the horses to sunbeams conveys their dazzling whiteness and splendour in a brief image.
Ulysses laughing as he drives the horses shows his relaxed confidence after a successful night raid.
